events.title: Jwalapuram (Kurnool): life before and after the Toba eruption
events.summary: Middle Palaeolithic stone tools at Jwalapuram in Kurnool district are found both below and above the ash of the Toba super-volcano (c. 74,000 years ago).
events.detail: The Jurreru valley at Jwalapuram preserves a thick bed of ash from the eruption of Toba in Sumatra. Tools of similar type above and below the ash suggest that people lived through the disaster. The Kurnool caves (Billa Surgam, Betamcherla) also have Stone Age bone tools and animal remains.
outcomes: Evidence that early humans in south India survived the Toba eruption.
events.yearHook: About 74,000 years ago, when the Toba super-volcano in Sumatra (Indonesia) blew up. The oldest date in Andhra history.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before:
People had been making stone tools in India for hundreds of thousands of years. This long time is the **Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic)**. People hunted animals, gathered plants and roots, and camped by rivers and in caves. They did not farm or keep animals yet.

Then, about 74,000 years ago, the **Toba** volcano in Sumatra erupted. It was the biggest eruption of the last two million years. Its ash blew across the Indian Ocean and fell as far away as the Kurnool hills.
events.after:
Life went on in the same hills. Later Stone Age people used the Kurnool caves (**Billa Surgam**, **Betamcherla**, **Muchatla Chintamani Gavi**) and made tools from bone, which is very rare.

The Stone Age has three stages. The **Old Stone Age** used big stone tools. The **Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic)** used tiny "microlith" tools. The **New Stone Age (Neolithic)** brought farming and cattle. The next event, the ash mounds of about 3000 BCE, is the New Stone Age.
events.today: Jwalapuram is in the Jurreru river valley of Kurnool district. The **Belum caves** (now in Nandyal district, which was carved out of Kurnool in 2022) are open to visitors. **Robert Bruce Foote**, the geologist who studied these caves in the 1880s, is called the father of Indian prehistory.
events.mnemonic: TOBA = "Tools On Both sides of the Ash": the same kind of tools lie below and above the ash, so people lived through it.

examAngle.point: The Billa Surgam caves are in Kurnool district.
examAngle.context: APPSC sets the trap with a nearby district, Anantapuramu. Learn the cluster: the Kurnool caves are Billa Surgam, Betamcherla and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi. Robert Bruce Foote explored Billa Surgam in the 1880s.

examAngle.point: Upper Palaeolithic bone tools in India come only from the Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi.
examAngle.context: Almost all Stone Age tools are stone, because bone rots away. The dry limestone caves of Kurnool kept bone tools safe. So these caves matter for all of India, not just AP.

examAngle.point: The Belum caves are the second-longest natural caves in India.
examAngle.context: The longest caves are in Meghalaya. Belum is the longest cave on the Indian plains. It lies near Kolimigundla in what is now Nandyal district.

events.title: Neolithic ash mounds of the southern Deccan
events.summary: From about 3000 BCE Neolithic cattle-herders of the southern Deccan leave huge ash mounds from burnt cattle dung, as at Utnur (Mahabubnagar) and Budihal (Karnataka).
events.detail: These pastoral communities of the Krishna–Tungabhadra region used polished stone axes, kept cattle in pens and periodically burnt the dung. Other Neolithic sites in Andhra and Telangana include Palavoy (Kurnool) and Veerapuram.
outcomes: Shows a cattle-based Neolithic culture in the south.
events.yearHook: About 3000 BCE, just before the Harappans build their great cities (about 2600 BCE).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: After the Stone Age hunters, people slowly learnt to tame animals and grow crops. This is the **New Stone Age (Neolithic)**. In the north-west it led to the Harappan cities. In the dry southern Deccan, the land of the **Krishna and Tungabhadra** rivers, people became cattle-keepers.
events.after: From about 1000 BCE these herders were joined by people who knew **iron** and buried their dead under big stones (the next event). Over many centuries these same black-soil plains became the heart of the Satavahana kingdom.
events.today: **Utnur** is in Mahabubnagar (now in Telangana). **Budihal** and **Sanganakallu** are in Karnataka. **Palavoy** is in Kurnool (AP). Experts still debate why the dung was burnt: as a festival fire, or to clean the cattle pens.
events.mnemonic: Ash mound = cattle dung + fire. Think "Utnur under ash".

events.title: Harappan trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha)
events.summary: Mesopotamian texts from about 2350 BCE mention contact with "Meluhha", probably the Harappan region, which sent carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and wood (NCERT).
events.detail: Harappan seals, weights, dice and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, and a Persian Gulf seal at Lothal. The Mesopotamian texts call Meluhha "a land of seafarers"; the Harappans traded through Oman (Magan) and Bahrain (Dilmun) (NCERT).
facts: Copper from Oman has traces of nickel similar to Harappan objects (NCERT).
events.yearHook: About 2350 BCE: the time of Sargon of Akkad in Mesopotamia.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"
events.before: The cities produced more than they needed: beads, cotton cloth, copper and timber.
events.after: When the cities declined (from 1900 BCE) this sea trade faded too.
events.today: Lothal (Gujarat) has what is often called the world's earliest known dockyard; a National Maritime Heritage Complex is being built there.

events.title: Megalithic burials in south India and Andhra
events.summary: From about 1000 BCE people in the Deccan and south India bury their dead in megaliths (big stones) with iron tools and black-and-red pottery (NCERT).
events.detail: Megaliths include stone circles, dolmens and cists; the dead were buried with pots, iron weapons and ornaments. NCERT notes that from c. 1000 BCE such burials were found across the Deccan, south India, the north-east and Kashmir, and that the goods buried showed differences in status. Andhra sites include Yeleswaram, Nagarjunakonda and Kadambapur.
outcomes: Iron came to the south with these communities.
events.yearHook: About 1000 BCE, the same time as the Later Vedic age in the north, when iron also came into use there.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: The New Stone Age cattle-herders of the Deccan were joined by people who knew how to make **iron**. Iron axes cut forests, and iron ploughs broke hard black soil far better than stone.
events.after: The megalith people's villages and iron farming are the base on which the first kingdoms of the south grew. These were the **Satavahanas** in the Deccan, and the **Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas** of the Sangam age in the Tamil land.
events.today: Megaliths still stand in many fields in AP. Experts group them by shape. A **dolmen** is a stone table. A **cist** is a stone box in a pit. A **stone circle** rings a grave. A **menhir** is one standing stone. A **sarcophagus** is a clay coffin, often on legs.
events.mnemonic: Megalith = mega (big) + lith (stone). "Big stone, iron bone": iron tools lie buried with the bones.

examAngle.point: Some megalithic graves have many goods and others almost none: a sign of rich and poor.
examAngle.context: NCERT uses megaliths to show that differences in status began early. Some graves have many pots, iron weapons and beads; others have almost nothing. APPSC turns this into a question about what megaliths tell us about society.

examAngle.point: Megalith types in AP: Tirupati has the largest group of human-shaped (anthropomorphic) burials. Chittoor and Anantapuramu have mostly sarcophagus burials. Krishna and Chittoor have many dolmens.
examAngle.context: APPSC 2025 asked which statement is wrong. The wrong one was "cist burials are most common in Visakhapatnam". Learn the right pairs, not the trap.

events.title: Persians conquer Gandhara
events.summary: Darius I of Persia conquers Gandhara and the Indus region around 518 BCE; it becomes the 20th and richest province of the Achaemenid empire.
events.detail: The Behistun inscription of Darius lists Gandhara and Hindush. The Persian contact brought the Kharosthi script (written right to left) and the Aramaic language to the north-west, and Indian soldiers fought in Persian armies against the Greeks.
outcomes: Taxila grew as a centre of learning.
events.yearHook: About 518 BCE: Darius I of Persia; about 190 years before Alexander (326 BCE).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: The north-west was split into small kingdoms such as Gandhara and Kamboja, open to the powerful Achaemenid Persians.
events.after: Persian rule brought the **Kharoshthi** script (from Aramaic) and the idea of carved royal inscriptions, which Ashoka later used. It also opened the route Alexander followed (326 BCE).
events.today: Ashoka's edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (Pakistan) are in Kharoshthi, a sign of the Persian legacy.

events.title: First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha
events.summary: Soon after the Buddha's death a council of monks meets at Rajagriha under Ajatashatru's patronage and Mahakassapa's presidency to collect his teachings.
events.detail: Upali recited the rules of the order (Vinaya Pitaka) and Ananda the discourses (Sutta Pitaka), according to Buddhist tradition. The Buddha's teachings were passed on orally and written down much later; the Tipitaka has three "baskets" (NCERT).
outcomes: Vinaya and Sutta Pitakas compiled orally.
facts: The Tipitaka has three baskets: Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 483 BCE, soon after the Buddha's death, at Rajagriha (capital of Magadha).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh); NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
events.before: When the Buddha died, nothing was written down. His monks feared his teachings would be lost or changed.
events.after: About 100 years later disputes over monks' rules led to the **Second Council** at Vaishali (383 BCE) and the first split.
events.today: The Saptaparni cave at Rajgir (Bihar) is shown as the place where the council met.

examAngle.point: First Council: Rajagriha, under King Ajatashatru, president Mahakassapa. Upali recited the Vinaya (rules) and Ananda the Sutta (sermons).
examAngle.context: Learn the councils as a set of four, each with a place, king and president. Councils 1 and 2 are in the time of the Haryanka and Shishunaga kings of Magadha; 3 under Ashoka; 4 under Kanishka.

events.title: Bindusara succeeds Chandragupta
events.summary: Chandragupta Maurya abdicates and becomes a Jaina monk; his son Bindusara becomes emperor (c. 297 BCE).
events.detail: Bindusara is said to have extended the empire into the Deccan. He kept contact with the Seleucids; Deimachus came as ambassador. His son Ashoka was governor of Ujjain and Taxila before winning the succession.
outcomes: Ashoka succeeded him after a struggle (c. 268 BCE).
events.yearHook: 297 BCE: Chandragupta gives up the throne after 24 years (321 − 24 = 297).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: **Chandragupta Maurya** became a Jain monk and went south with **Bhadrabahu**; tradition says he died at **Shravanabelagola** (Karnataka) by fasting.
events.after: Bindusara pushed the empire into the Deccan. His son **Ashoka**, governor at Ujjain and Taxila, took the throne after a struggle (268 BCE, next event).
events.today: Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola has the Chandragupta basadi.
events.mnemonic: Bindusara = "Amitraghata" (slayer of foes); Greeks called him Amitrochates.

events.title: Kharavela of Kalinga and the Hathigumpha inscription
events.summary: Kharavela, the Jaina king of Kalinga, records his reign year by year in the Hathigumpha ("elephant cave") inscription at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar (c. 1st century BCE).
events.detail: The inscription says he repaired a canal first dug by a Nanda king, sent his army west against the Satavahana Satakarni, and attacked Magadha, bringing back a Jaina image taken by the Nandas. The Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves were made for Jaina monks.
outcomes: Kalinga became a strong Jaina kingdom.
events.yearHook: About the 1st century BCE: about 200 years after Ashoka's Kalinga war (261 BCE).

participants.role: The Nandas had dug the canal and taken the Jaina image.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: The Ranigumpha cave at Udayagiri is the finest of the Jaina caves.
events.before: After Ashoka's death Kalinga became free again under the **Chedi (Mahameghavahana)** dynasty.
events.after: Kharavela raided Magadha and the south, and fought the Satavahana **Satakarni**. After him Kalinga fades from records for a long time.
events.today: The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were cut for Jain monks in his time.
events.mnemonic: Hathigumpha = "elephant cave". Kharavela = Kalinga's Jain king who dated his deeds year by year.

events.title: Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription
events.summary: The Shaka ruler Rudradaman I records in Sanskrit (c. 150 CE) that he repaired the Sudarshana lake, built under Chandragupta Maurya and improved under Ashoka (NCERT).
events.detail: It is the first long inscription in chaste Sanskrit. It says a storm broke the dam and the king repaired it from his own treasury without forced labour or extra taxes (NCERT). He also claims to have twice defeated Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha, but spared him because of a relationship.
outcomes: Sanskrit became the language of royal inscriptions.
facts: The same rock has an Ashokan edict.
Shaka rulers: Maues (Moga), Azilises, Chastana (Ujjain), Nahapana and Rudradaman; Suvishakha was Rudradaman's Pahlava governor who repaired the dam.
Shaka rulers took the titles Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa.
Parthians (Pahlavas): Gondophernes (Gondophares) — Takht-i-Bahi inscription (45 CE); St Thomas came in his time.
events.yearHook: About 150 CE: about 44 years after Gautamiputra Satakarni (106 CE).

participants.role: The lake was built in his time (NCERT).
The lake was improved in his time (NCERT).
Repaired the lake again in the 5th century.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
events.before: The Shaka **Western Kshatrapas** of Ujjain (Kardamaka line, founded by **Chastana**) rose as the Satavahanas weakened in the west.
events.after: Rudradaman twice beat a Satavahana king (spared as a relative). His line ruled until **Chandragupta II** of the Guptas ended it (about 400 CE).
events.today: The inscription is the first long one in classical **Sanskrit**. It records repairs to the **Sudarshana lake**, first built under Chandragupta Maurya by his governor Pushyagupta.
events.mnemonic: Junagadh rock = three kings on one rock: Ashoka's edicts, Rudradaman's inscription (150 CE), Skandagupta's inscription (about 457 CE).

events.title: Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya
events.summary: In 499 CE Aryabhata, aged 23, writes the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura (Pataliputra), stating that the earth rotates on its axis and explaining eclipses (NCERT).
events.detail: He gave the place-value system a firm base, a value of pi close to 3.1416, and rules for squares, cubes and roots. He said day and night were caused by the earth's rotation and that eclipses happen because of the shadows of the earth and moon, not because of Rahu (NCERT). Varahamihira (Panchasiddhantika, Brihatsamhita) and Brahmagupta came later.
outcomes: Basis of Indian astronomy; India's first satellite named after him (1975).
events.yearHook: 499 CE — one year short of 500.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Gupta peace and patronage helped science. Indians had used a place-value system with nine numerals; the idea of **zero** as a number was taking shape.
events.after: **Varahamihira** (about 550) and **Brahmagupta** (628, rules for zero) followed. Arab scholars carried Indian numerals to Europe, where they are still called "Arabic numerals".
events.today: India's first satellite (1975) and a research institute in Nainital (ARIES) are named after him.
events.mnemonic: Indian astronomers in order "A-V-B-B": Aryabhata 499, Varahamihira about 550, Brahmagupta 628, Bhaskara II 1150 (Lilavati).

events.title: Vakatakas and the Ajanta paintings
events.summary: Under the Vakataka king Harishena (c. 460–478 CE) many of the Ajanta caves are cut and painted with scenes from the Jatakas (NCERT shows Ajanta paintings).
events.detail: The Vakatakas ruled the Deccan and were allies of the Guptas: Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavati married Rudrasena II. Ajanta has 29 rock-cut Buddhist caves; the paintings in caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 are the finest. The site was rediscovered by a British officer in 1819.

alsoOn.text: Ajanta caves rediscovered by a British officer, John Smith.

events.yearHook: About 475 CE: between Fa-Hien (405) and Aryabhata (499).

participants.role: His daughter married into the Vakataka family.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: The **Vakatakas** ruled the Deccan as Gupta in-laws. Ajanta had older caves of the 2nd century BCE.
events.after: Later painting traditions such as **Bagh** (MP) and **Sittanavasal** (Tamil Nadu) follow Ajanta's style.
events.today: Ajanta (Maharashtra) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983; the Bodhisattva Padmapani of Cave 1 is its most famous painting.

events.title: Hunas and Yashodharman
events.summary: The Huna (White Hun) kings Toramana and Mihirakula conquer the north-west; Yashodharman of Malwa defeats Mihirakula around 528 CE, as his Mandsaur pillar records.
events.detail: Skandagupta had pushed back an earlier Huna attack (c. 455–460 CE). Toramana conquered Punjab and Malwa about 500 CE. His son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala and persecuted Buddhists. Gupta power broke up under the strain.
outcomes: Decline of the Guptas; rise of regional kingdoms (Maukharis, Pushyabhutis).
events.yearHook: About 528 CE: Yashodharman beats Mihirakula.

participants.role: Had held back the first Huna attack.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Skandagupta had stopped the Hunas once (about 455 CE), but the empire weakened after him.
events.after: The north broke into regional kingdoms: Maukharis of **Kanauj**, Pushyabhutis of **Thanesar**, later Guptas of Magadha, Maitrakas of **Vallabhi**. Out of these came **Harsha** (606 CE).
events.today: Mihirakula is remembered in Kalhana's **Rajatarangini** as a cruel king of Kashmir.

events.title: Salankayanas of Vengi
events.summary: After the Ikshvakus, the Salankayanas rule from Vengi (near Eluru) in the Krishna–Godavari delta (c. 300–440 CE); their king Hastivarman is defeated by Samudragupta (Prayaga prashasti).
events.detail:
They issued copper-plate charters in Prakrit and later Sanskrit and worshipped Chitraratha Swami (the Sun). The Brihatphalayanas (Kudura) and Anandagotrikas (Guntur) were small dynasties of the same age. Vengi later became the capital of the Eastern Chalukyas.

The early Pallavas also ruled parts of southern Andhra, issuing Prakrit charters such as the Mayidavolu plates of Shivaskandavarman; Vishnugopa of Kanchi was another king defeated by Samudragupta.
outcomes: Followed by the Vishnukundins; Vengi became the Eastern Chalukya capital.
events.yearHook: About 320 CE, the same year the Gupta empire begins (Chandragupta I, 320 CE).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: With the Ikshvakus gone (about 300 CE), coastal Andhra broke into small kingdoms. The **Salankayanas** held **Vengi**, the rich land between the Krishna and the Godavari.
events.after: Samudragupta's march to the south (about 350 CE) defeated Hastivarman of Vengi and Vishnugopa of Kanchi. He let them keep their thrones as kings who paid him tribute. The **Vishnukundins** (from about 420 CE) then took the region. In 624 CE Vengi became the capital of the **Eastern Chalukyas** for about 450 years.
events.today: Old Vengi is **Pedavegi**, near Eluru. Samudragupta's list of beaten kings is carved on the **Allahabad (Prayaga) pillar**.
events.mnemonic: Samudragupta's southern list has two "V"s from our area: Vengi (Hastivarman) and Vishnugopa (Kanchi).

examAngle.point: The Manchikallu and Mayidavolu (Maidavolu) inscriptions belong to the Pallavas.
examAngle.context: Both are early Pallava records in Prakrit, found in the Krishna–Guntur region. The Mayidavolu plates are of **Shivaskandavarman**. They show the Pallavas started near the Krishna before moving to Kanchi.

events.title: Simhavishnu revives the Pallavas of Kanchi
events.summary: Simhavishnu (c. 575) ends the Kalabhra interlude and makes the Pallavas of Kanchi a great power; his son Mahendravarman I and grandson Narasimhavarman I fight the Badami Chalukyas (NCERT notes the rise of the Pallavas c. 500–600).
events.detail: The early Pallavas had issued Prakrit charters from the Andhra region. Kanchi became a great centre of learning (the ghatika). The Pallavas spread the Grantha script and Indian culture to Southeast Asia. The Cholas ended Pallava rule (c. 897).
events.yearHook: c. 575 → Vatapi 642 → Cholas c. 897.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Later Pallavas: Nandivarman II built the Vaikuntha Perumal temple, Kanchi; Aparajitavarman was the last, defeated by the Cholas.
Mahendravarman I defeated Pulakeshin II at Pullalur (by Pallava claim).
events.before: After the Sangam age (about 300 CE) the **Kalabhras** ruled the Tamil land. The early Pallavas had ruled the Krishna region of Andhra, issuing Prakrit charters (Mayidavolu, Manchikallu).
events.after: His son **Mahendravarman I** (about 610) began rock-cut temples; grandson **Narasimhavarman I** sacked Vatapi (642).
events.today: Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital, is still called the "city of a thousand temples".

events.title: Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, teaches four vows
events.summary: Parshvanatha, a prince of Varanasi, teaches a simple path of four vows about 250 years before Mahavira. He is the earliest Tirthankara most historians accept as a real person.
events.detail:
Jains believe in **24 Tirthankaras** ("ford-makers": teachers who show the way across the river of rebirth). The first is **Rishabhanatha** (symbol: bull). Most of them belong to legend. **Parshvanatha**, the 23rd (symbol: snake), is different: he is placed in history, about the 8th century BCE.

He was the son of **King Ashvasena of Varanasi (Kashi)**. He taught **four vows**: non-violence (ahimsa), truth (satya), not stealing (asteya) and owning nothing (aparigraha). He attained nirvana at **Sammed Shikhar** (Parasnath hill, Jharkhand), where Jains say 20 of the 24 Tirthankaras died.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I Ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes (Jainism)
facts: Parshvanatha believed in the eternity of matter.
events.yearHook: About 800 BCE: roughly 250 years before Mahavira (born 599 BCE in the Jain count).
events.before: In the **Later Vedic age** (about 1000–600 BCE) religion was full of costly sacrifices run by Brahmana priests. Some thinkers began to look for a path of self-control instead of rituals.
events.after: About 250 years later **Mahavira** took up Parshvanatha's order, added a fifth vow and gave Jainism its present form (next events).
events.today: Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hill) in Jharkhand is the holiest Jain pilgrimage site. Parshvanatha's images show a many-headed snake over his head.
events.mnemonic: Parshva's FOUR, Mahavira's FIVE: the vow Mahavira added was Brahmacharya. Symbols in order: "Bull → Snake → Lion" (1st, 23rd, 24th).

events.title: Mahavira attains Kaivalya and starts preaching
events.summary: After 12 years of hard penance, Mahavira attains Kevala Jnana (Kaivalya, "supreme knowledge") at 42, under a sal tree at Jrimbhikagrama on the river Rijupalika. For the next 30 years he teaches the Jain path.
events.detail:
From now on he is called **Jina** ("the conqueror", of his own senses) — so his followers are **Jainas**. He is also **Kevalin** (the all-knowing one) and **Nirgrantha** ("free of bonds").

He taught in **Ardhamagadhi Prakrit**, the people's language, not Sanskrit. His main teachings:

- **Five great vows** (Pancha Mahavrata) for monks: the four of Parshvanatha plus **Brahmacharya** (celibacy). Householders keep a milder form, the **Anuvratas** (small vows).
- **Three jewels** (Triratna): right faith, right knowledge, right conduct.
- **Anekantavada** (truth has many sides) and **Syadvada** ("maybe": every statement is true only from some point of view).
- The world has **jiva** (soul) and **ajiva** (matter); even stones and water have life; karma sticks to the soul and penance burns it away.
- **No creator God**: gods exist but rank below the Jina.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I Ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes (Jainism)
facts: Umaswati wrote the Tattvartha Sutra; Acharya Kundakunda wrote the Samayasara.
events.yearHook: About 557 BCE in the Jain count: born 599, Kaivalya at 42, so 599 − 42 = 557. (Historians who use 540 BCE for his birth get 498.)

participants.role: Attains Kaivalya and begins to teach.

events.before: Mahavira left home at 30 and wandered for 12 years as a naked ascetic, fasting and in silence. For about six years **Makkhali Gosala** travelled with him; Gosala later founded the **Ajivika** sect.
events.after: He preached for 30 years in **Magadha, Kosala and Mithila** and gathered **eleven Ganadharas** (chief disciples), the first being **Indrabhuti Gautama**. His son-in-law **Jamali** later led the first split in the order. He died at **Pavapuri** at 72 (next event).
events.today: Jain monks still keep the five vows; Svetambara monks of some sub-sects wear a **muhapatti** (mouth cloth) so as not to harm tiny creatures. Gandhi's idea of non-violence owed much to Jain ahimsa.
events.mnemonic: Mahavira's ages "30-42-72": left home at 30, Kaivalya at 42, nirvana at 72. Five vows "A-SABA": Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, Aparigraha.

examAngle.point: Jainism: Triratna; Buddhism: the Eightfold Path (Ashtanga Marga); Shaivism: the linga; animism: nature worship.
examAngle.context: APPSC pairs each faith with its key idea. The Triratna is the Jain path to freedom (moksha); do not confuse it with the Buddhist "three jewels" (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha), which is a different idea with the same name.

examAngle.point: Early Jainas preached in Prakrit and gave up Sanskrit; the canon is in Ardhamagadhi; later works used Apabhramsa, Kannada and Tamil.
examAngle.context: Using the people's language is one reason Jainism (like Buddhism) spread among traders and farmers. Later the Jains also wrote much early Kannada and Tamil literature.

events.title: Mahavira's nirvana at Pavapuri
events.summary: Mahavira dies at Pavapuri (near Rajgir, Bihar) at the age of 72, in 527 BCE by the Jain count (468 BCE by another). Arya Sudharma becomes the first head of the order.
events.detail: Of the eleven Ganadharas only **Arya Sudharma** survived him and became the first **Thera** (head) of the Jain order. The faith spread with royal help: **Udayin**, who followed Ajatashatru on the Magadha throne, was a Jaina, and the **Nanda** age had the teachers Sambhutavijaya and Bhadrabahu.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I Ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes (Jainism)
events.yearHook: 527 BCE in the Jain count: 599 − 72 = 527. About 44 years before the Buddha's death (483 BCE).
events.before: Mahavira had preached for 30 years after his Kaivalya (about 557 BCE), mostly in Magadha, the rising kingdom of Bimbisara and Ajatashatru.
events.after: The order grew in Magadha. In the Mauryan age a famine sent **Bhadrabahu** south with **Chandragupta Maurya**, and the order split into **Digambaras** and **Svetambaras** (about 300 BCE, next event).
events.today: Pavapuri has the **Jal Mandir**, a white temple in the middle of a lotus pond, built where he was cremated. Jains mark his nirvana at **Diwali**.
events.mnemonic: Pava for Mahavira, Kushinagar for the Buddha: "P for the Prophet of ahimsa, K for the Kind teacher".

events.title: Second Jain council at Vallabhi writes down the canon
events.summary: The second Jain council at Vallabhi (Gujarat), under Devardhigani Kshamashramana, writes down the Svetambara canon: the 12 Angas and 12 Upangas, in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.
events.detail:
For about 1,000 years the teachings had been learnt by heart. The first council at **Pataliputra** (about 300 BCE) had only arranged them into the **12 Angas**. At **Vallabhi** they were finally **written down**, with the Upangas and other texts added.

The Digambaras do not accept this canon: they say the original texts (the 14 **Purvas**, kept inside the 12th Anga) were lost.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I Ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes (Jainism)
events.yearHook: 512 CE (some books give 453–454 CE). Same century as the Maitrakas of Vallabhi and the late Guptas.
events.before: The first council at Pataliputra (about 300 BCE) had grouped the teachings into 12 Angas, but they were still passed on by memory and parts were being forgotten.
events.after: Written texts let Jain learning flourish in Gujarat and Rajasthan under later kings (for example **Hemachandra** at the court of the Chalukya king **Kumarapala**, 12th century).
events.today: Vallabhi (Vala, near Bhavnagar, Gujarat) was also a famous centre of learning, called the rival of Nalanda.
events.mnemonic: Councils: "Pataliputra Puts in order (300 BCE, Sthulabhadra); Vallabhi Writes it down (512 CE, Devardhigani)".

events.title: Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir: Mahayana takes shape
events.summary: Under the Kushana king Kanishka a council meets at Kundalvana in Kashmir, led by Vasumitra with Ashvaghosha as deputy. Its texts are in Sanskrit, and the split between Mahayana and Hinayana (Theravada) becomes sharp.
events.detail:
Until now Buddhists had worshipped the Buddha only through **symbols** (the wheel, the tree, footprints) and aimed at their own release. The **Mahayana** ("great vehicle") now worshipped the Buddha in human images and honoured **Bodhisattvas**, beings who put off their own nirvana to help others (Avalokiteshvara, Maitreya, Manjushri).

The older school, which kept the Pali texts and the old way, was called **Hinayana** ("lesser vehicle", a name given by its rivals) or **Theravada** ("teaching of the elders"). Later, in eastern India and Tibet, came **Vajrayana** (the "thunderbolt vehicle", with magic and rituals).

The council wrote commentaries called **Vibhasha** (the Mahavibhasha).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I Ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes (Buddhism)
facts: Mahayana Bodhisattvas: Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani), Maitreya (the future Buddha), Manjushri; the six Paramitas (perfections).
Vajrayana (Tantric Buddhism) grew later in eastern India and Tibet.
events.yearHook: About 100 CE (books give from 72 CE to the end of the 1st century). Kanishka took the throne in 78 CE, the start of the Shaka era.
events.before: Ashoka's **Third Council** (about 250 BCE) had sent monks abroad. In the north-west, Greek, Shaka and Kushana rulers met Buddhism. Their artists began to show the Buddha in human form (Gandhara and Mathura).
events.after: Mahayana spread along the **Silk Road** to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan; Theravada went to Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand. Andhra teachers such as **Acharya Nagarjuna** shaped Mahayana thought.
events.today: The world's two main Buddhist families still follow this split: Theravada in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, Mahayana in China, Japan, Korea and Tibet.
events.mnemonic: Councils "R-V-P-K" = Rajagriha (483 BCE), Vaishali (383 BCE), Pataliputra (250 BCE), Kashmir (about 100 CE). Every 100 years or so. Presidents "Maha-Saba-Mogga-Vasu": Mahakassapa, Sabakami, Moggaliputta Tissa, Vasumitra.

events.title: Ajatashatru takes the throne of Magadha and beats Kosala and the Vajjis
events.summary: Ajatashatru (about 492–460 BCE) seizes the throne from his father Bimbisara, wars down Kosala and the Vajji republic of Vaishali, and builds a fort at Pataligrama on the Ganga.
events.detail:
Buddhist and Jain texts say he imprisoned and starved his father. He fought his uncle **Prasenajit of Kosala** and won Kashi. Against the **Vajji confederacy** (the Lichchhavis of Vaishali) he used two new war engines: the **mahashilakantaka** (a catapult for big stones) and the **rathamusala** (a chariot with a swinging mace). His minister **Vassakara** split the Vajjis from within.

He built a small fort, **Pataligrama**, where the Son meets the Ganga; it grew into **Pataliputra**. He was the patron of the **First Buddhist Council** at Rajagriha (483 BCE).
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 11; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 492 BCE: Bimbisara (544) + 52 years. The Buddha dies in his reign (483 BCE).
events.before: **Bimbisara** (544–492 BCE) had made Magadha strong through marriage alliances (Kosala, Lichchhavi and Madra princesses) and by taking **Anga**.
events.after: His son **Udayin** moved the capital to **Pataliputra** (about 460 BCE). After the Haryankas came the **Shishunagas** (about 413 BCE) and the **Nandas** (345 BCE).
events.today: Rajgir (Bihar) still has the "Bimbisara jail" and the cyclopean wall, a stone wall about 40 km long around old Rajagriha.
events.mnemonic: Haryanka kings "B-A-U": Bimbisara (544), Ajatashatru (492), Udayin (460). Each "kills his father" story repeats, so the Haryankas are called a dynasty of parricides.

events.title: Udayin makes Pataliputra the capital of Magadha
events.summary: Udayin (about 460–444 BCE), son of Ajatashatru, shifts the capital from Rajagriha to Pataliputra, at the meeting of the Ganga and the Son.
events.detail:
Rajagriha was safe inside five hills, but far from the river trade routes. **Pataliputra** (modern Patna) stood where rivers met, so it was easy to defend and good for trade and moving troops by boat. It stayed the capital of the Nandas, the Mauryas and, much later, the Guptas.

Udayin was a follower of Jainism.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 11; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 460 BCE: 84 years after Bimbisara (544) and about 140 years before the Mauryas (321).
events.before: **Ajatashatru** had built a fort at Pataligrama on the Ganga during his war with the Vajjis.
events.after: The Haryankas ended about 413 BCE, when the people put **Shishunaga** on the throne (next event).
events.today: Patna, the capital of Bihar, stands on the site. Excavations at Kumrahar show the Mauryan pillared hall of Pataliputra.
events.mnemonic: Magadha capitals in order: "Girivraja/Rajagriha → Pataliputra → (Vaishali for a while under Shishunaga) → Pataliputra again".

events.title: Shishunaga dynasty: Avanti is absorbed into Magadha
events.summary: Shishunaga, a minister, replaces the last Haryanka king (about 413 BCE). He destroys the power of Avanti, Magadha's chief rival, and briefly rules from Vaishali.
events.detail: With **Avanti** (Ujjain) gone, Magadha had no rival left among the Mahajanapadas. His son **Kalashoka (Kakavarna)** took the capital back to Pataliputra and held the **Second Buddhist Council** at Vaishali (383 BCE).
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 11; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 413 BCE; the Second Buddhist Council (383) falls in Kalashoka's reign; the Nandas take over in 345.
events.before: The last Haryanka kings were weak; the people deposed them.
events.after: About 345 BCE **Mahapadma Nanda** seized power and built the first great empire of the Ganga plain (next Magadha event).
events.today: Vaishali (Bihar) has the Ashokan lion pillar and the Second Council site.

events.title: Alexander's army refuses at the Beas; retreat and death at Babylon
events.summary: At the Beas (Hyphasis) in 326 BCE Alexander's tired soldiers refuse to go further east. He turns back down the Indus and through the Makran desert, and dies at Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32.
events.detail:
The soldiers had marched for years and had heard of the huge army of the **Nandas** beyond the Beas. Alexander divided his Indian conquests among governors (satraps). After his death his empire split among his generals; **Seleucus Nicator** took the eastern part.

Within a few years **Chandragupta Maurya** drove out the Greek governors of the north-west.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 11; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 323 BCE: three years after Hydaspes (326) and two years after Chandragupta Maurya rises (321 BCE in NCERT).
events.before: In 326 BCE Alexander beat **Porus** at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) and pushed east to the Beas.
events.after: The power vacuum in the north-west helped **Chandragupta Maurya** (321 BCE). In 305 BCE Seleucus fought Chandragupta and made a treaty, giving him the north-west for 500 elephants.
events.today: Greek writers who came with him (Nearchus, Onesicritus, Aristobulus) are early sources for India. Many river names come from Greek: Hydaspes (Jhelum), Hyphasis (Beas), Akesines (Chenab).
events.mnemonic: Alexander in India "3-2-6 to 3-2-3": Hydaspes 326, retreat 325, death 323. Two years later, Mauryas (321).

events.title: Menander (Milinda), the greatest Indo-Greek king
events.summary: Menander I (about 165–130 BCE) rules the Indo-Greek kingdom from Sakala (Sialkot). His talks with the Buddhist monk Nagasena are recorded in the Pali text Milindapanho ("Questions of Milinda").
events.detail:
Menander pushed into the Ganga valley; Patanjali and the Gargi Samhita mention Yavana raids reaching Saketa and Madhyamika. In the Milindapanho he asks about rebirth, the soul and karma, and in the end is said to accept Buddhism.

Indo-Greek coins are the first in India with clear **portraits** of kings and inscriptions in two languages (Greek and Kharoshthi Prakrit), and the first well-made **gold** coins.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 155 BCE: about 30 years after Pushyamitra Shunga takes Pataliputra (185 BCE).
events.before: After the Mauryas fell (185 BCE), Greek rulers of **Bactria** (north Afghanistan), led by **Demetrius**, crossed the Hindu Kush into the Punjab (about 180 BCE).
events.after: Later Indo-Greek kings were weaker; one of them, **Antialcidas**, sent an envoy to a Shunga king (about 110 BCE, next event). By the 1st century BCE the **Shakas** had overrun them.
events.today: Sialkot (Sakala) is in Pakistani Punjab. Indo-Greek coins are a main source for the period, because few texts survive.
events.mnemonic: Indo-Greek kings in order "D-M-A": Demetrius (about 180 BCE), Menander (about 155), Antialcidas (about 110, Heliodorus pillar).

events.title: Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar: a Greek worships Vasudeva
events.summary: Heliodorus, envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the Shunga king Bhagabhadra, sets up a Garuda pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha) in honour of Vasudeva (Krishna), calling himself a Bhagavata.
events.detail:
It is one of the earliest stone records of **Bhagavatism**, the worship of Vasudeva-Krishna that grew into **Vaishnavism**. It shows that foreigners also took up Indian religions.

It also shows that the Shungas and the Indo-Greeks, once enemies, now sent envoys to each other.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 113 BCE: about 70 years after Pushyamitra (185 BCE).
events.before: The **Shunga** kings ruled from Vidisha and Pataliputra and backed the old Vedic religion, while devotion (bhakti) to gods like Vasudeva was growing.
events.after: Bhagavata worship spread under the Guptas, who called themselves **Parama-bhagavata** (great devotees of Vishnu).
events.today: The pillar (locally "Khamba Baba") stands at Besnagar near Vidisha, MP, close to Sanchi.

events.title: Vasudeva Kanva ends the Shungas: the Kanva dynasty
events.summary: Vasudeva, a Brahmana minister, kills the last Shunga king Devabhuti (about 73 BCE) and founds the short Kanva dynasty, which lasts until about 28 BCE, when the Satavahanas end it.
events.detail: Only four Kanva kings ruled, for about 45 years, over a small area around Magadha. The Puranas say the **Satavahanas** (the "Andhras") ended them.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 73 BCE to 28 BCE: 45 years. "Shungas 112 years, Kanvas 45 years".
events.before: The Shungas (185–73 BCE) had grown weak after Pushyamitra and Agnimitra.
events.after: The Satavahanas (from about 230 BCE in the Deccan) ended the Kanvas about 28 BCE. North India then lay open to the Shakas and Kushanas.
events.mnemonic: After the Mauryas: "Shunga Killed, Kanva Kept briefly, Satavahana Swallowed".

events.title: The Shakas arrive: Maues rules Gandhara and Taxila
events.summary: The Shakas (Scythians), pushed out of Central Asia by the Yuezhi, enter India and take over the Indo-Greek lands. Maues (Moga) is the first Shaka king in the north-west (about 85 BCE).
events.detail:
The Shakas set up five branches: in **Afghanistan**, **Taxila** (Punjab), **Mathura**, western India (**Kshaharatas**, under Nahapana) and the Deccan/Ujjain (**Kardamakas**, under Chastana and later **Rudradaman**). Their governors were called **Kshatrapas** (satraps) and **Mahakshatrapas**.

Tradition says a king of Ujjain, **Vikramaditya**, drove the Shakas back in 57 BCE, starting the **Vikram Samvat**.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 85 BCE: about 30 years before the Vikram Samvat (57 BCE) and about 160 years before the Shaka era (78 CE).
events.before: The **Indo-Greeks** (from about 180 BCE) had split into small kingdoms. Far to the north, the **Yuezhi** were driving the Shakas out of their grazing lands.
events.after: Western Shaka rulers (the **Western Kshatrapas**) lasted until **Chandragupta II** of the Guptas ended them (about 400 CE). In the north the **Parthians** (Pahlavas) followed (Gondophernes, about 20 CE).
events.today: The Shakas brought trousers, long coats and boots, and new cavalry skills to India.
events.mnemonic: Who pushed whom: "Yuezhi push Shakas, Shakas push Greeks" — a chain of Central Asian peoples moving south.

events.title: Gondophernes, the Indo-Parthian king, and St Thomas
events.summary: Gondophernes (about 20–46 CE) rules the Indo-Parthian (Pahlava) kingdom of the north-west. Christian tradition says the apostle St Thomas came to his court.
events.detail: The **Parthians** (Pahlavas) came from Iran. The **Takht-i-Bahi inscription** (near Peshawar) names Gondophernes. Their rule was short; the **Kushanas** soon took over the north-west.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 20 CE: a few years before Kujula Kadphises founds the Kushana kingdom (about 30 CE).
events.before: The Shakas (from about 85 BCE) held the north-west; the Parthians pushed in from Iran.
events.after: The **Kushanas** under **Kujula Kadphises** (about 30 CE) ended Parthian rule.
events.today: Takht-i-Bahi is a UNESCO site in Pakistan. Kerala's St Thomas Christians trace their faith to St Thomas (said to have come about 52 CE).

events.title: Kujula Kadphises founds the Kushana empire
events.summary: Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushana clan of the Yuezhi, unites them and takes the north-west (about 30 CE). His son Vima Kadphises issues the first big gold coins of India and calls himself a devotee of Shiva (Maheshvara).
events.detail:
The **Yuezhi** were nomads from north-west China, driven west by the Xiongnu. One of their five clans, the **Kushanas**, became an empire stretching from Central Asia to the Ganga valley.

Vima's gold coins followed the Roman **aureus** in weight, a sign of the rich Roman trade.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 30 CE; Kanishka takes the throne about 78 CE (the Shaka era).
events.before: Shakas (from about 85 BCE) and Parthians (about 20 CE) ruled the north-west by turns.
events.after: **Kanishka** (78 CE) made the empire greatest: Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura were its capitals (next event).
events.today: The Rabatak inscription (Afghanistan, found 1993) gives the order of the Kushana kings.
events.mnemonic: Kushana kings "K-V-K": Kujula Kadphises, Vima Kadphises, Kanishka. "Kadphises Kings before Kanishka".

events.title: Indo-Roman trade at its height: Arikamedu, Muziris and the Periplus
events.summary: Roman ships use the monsoon winds to sail to India. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (about 60 CE) lists Indian ports; Roman gold coins pour into south India in return for pepper, pearls, muslin and spices.
events.detail:
The Greek sailor **Hippalus** is said to have learnt the monsoon winds (about 45 CE), so ships could cross the Arabian Sea directly. Ports included **Barygaza (Bharuch)**, **Muziris** (Kerala), **Arikamedu** (near Puducherry, a Roman-style trading station) and the Andhra ports of **Ghantasala** and **Motupalli**.

Pliny the Elder complained that India drained Rome of 50 million sesterces a year. Indian guilds (**shrenis**) grew rich, and Buddhist monasteries on trade routes got their gifts.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 60 CE: between Kujula Kadphises (30) and Kanishka (78).
events.before: After the Mauryas, India had many kingdoms but busy roads and ports. The Roman empire under Augustus (from 27 BCE) wanted Indian luxuries.
events.after: Trade fell in the 3rd century CE when Rome was in crisis. This hit the Satavahanas and the guild-funded Buddhist sites; no later rulers issued ship coins.
events.today: Hoards of Roman coins are found all over south India, including Andhra. Arikamedu and Pattanam (Muziris) are excavated sites.
events.mnemonic: "Pepper to Rome, gold to India": Romans called pepper "yavanapriya" (dear to the Yavanas).

events.title: Kushana power fades under Persian (Sassanian) pressure
events.summary: After Vasudeva I (about 190–230 CE), the last great Kushana, the Sassanian kings of Persia take Bactria and the north-west. Small Kushana chiefs survive until the Guptas.
events.detail: The **Sassanians** (from 224 CE) built a strong Persian empire and turned the Kushana lands in Afghanistan into "Kushanshahr", ruled by Sassanian princes. In India, local powers (Nagas, Yaudheyas, Malavas) rose until the **Guptas** united the north (320 CE).
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 230 CE: about 90 years before the Guptas begin (320 CE).
events.before: Kanishka's heirs (Huvishka, Vasudeva I) held a big but loose empire.
events.after: The north was divided for about a century, until **Chandragupta I** founded the Gupta empire (320 CE).

events.title: Hala, the poet-king, compiles the Gathasaptasati
events.summary: Hala, the 17th Satavahana king, gathers 700 short love poems in Maharashtri Prakrit: the Gathasaptasati (Gaha Sattasai), the best window on Satavahana village life.
events.detail:
The poems speak of farmers, herders, festivals, seasons and love, in simple Prakrit. Hala's court also had **Gunadhya**, who wrote the **Brihatkatha** (a huge story collection, now lost) in **Paishachi** Prakrit, and **Sarvavarma**, who wrote the **Katantra**, a short Sanskrit grammar.

A Telugu legend says Hala married **Lilavati**, a princess of Sri Lanka; the Prakrit poem **Lilavai** (Lilavati Parinayam) by **Kutuhala** tells this story.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 20 CE (1st century CE): between the founding (about 230 BCE) and Gautamiputra (about 106 CE).
events.before: The early Satavahanas (Simuka, Kanha, Satakarni I) built the kingdom in the western Deccan. In the 1st century CE the **Shakas** began to press on their west.
events.after: Soon after Hala the Shaka **Nahapana** took the western lands; **Gautamiputra Satakarni** won them back (about 106 CE).
events.today: Telugu and Marathi writers both claim the Gathasaptasati as an early ancestor; some of its words are early Telugu.
events.mnemonic: Hala's court "G-S-K": Gunadhya (Brihatkatha), Sarvavarma (Katantra), Kutuhala (Lilavai).

events.title: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi: the Satavahanas move east to Andhra
events.summary: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi (about 130–154 CE), son of Gautamiputra, rules from Dhanyakataka (Amaravati) on the Krishna. From now the Satavahana heartland is Andhra.
events.detail:
Pressed by the Shaka **Western Kshatrapas** in the west, the later kings made the east their base. Inscriptions of Pulumavi are found at **Amaravati**, and his coins carry ships with two masts — the sea trade of the Krishna-Godavari ports such as **Ghantasala** and **Motupalli**.

The Shaka king **Rudradaman** (Junagadh inscription, about 150 CE) says he twice beat a Satavahana king but spared him because they were related by marriage.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 130 CE: about 24 years after Gautamiputra (106 CE) and 20 years before Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription (150).
events.before: **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (about 106 CE) had won back the west from Nahapana, but the Shakas of Ujjain stayed strong.
events.after: The great stupa of **Amaravati** was enlarged in this age (about 150 CE). The last great king, **Yajna Sri Satakarni** (about 175 CE), won back some western land (next Satavahana event).
events.today: Dharanikota, near Amaravati (Palnadu), is old Dhanyakataka; the ship coins are in the Amaravati and Chennai museums.
events.mnemonic: Satavahana capitals "west to east": Pratishthana (Paithan) → Dhanyakataka (Amaravati). "P to D".

events.title: Yajna Sri Satakarni, the last great Satavahana
events.summary: Yajna Sri Satakarni (about 170–200 CE) wins back parts of the west from the Shakas and issues coins with ships. After him the Satavahana kingdom breaks up.
events.detail: After his death the kingdom split among feudatories: the **Ikshvakus** in the Krishna valley (Andhra), the **Abhiras** in Maharashtra, the **Chutus** in Karnataka and others. Roman trade was falling, which also weakened them.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 175 CE; the Ikshvakus take Vijayapuri about 50 years later (225 CE).
events.before: Under **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** (about 130 CE) the kingdom had moved its centre to Andhra.
events.after: The **Ikshvakus** (about 225 CE) followed in Andhra, and **Vakatakas** later in the western Deccan.
events.today: He is the last Satavahana king whose coins are found widely, from Gujarat to Andhra.

events.title: Cheran Senguttuvan and the Kannagi temple: the Gajabahu link
events.summary: The Chera king Senguttuvan ("the Red Chera") builds a temple to Kannagi, the heroine of the Silappadikaram. The Sri Lankan king Gajabahu I is said to attend; since Gajabahu ruled about 171–193 CE, this dates the Sangam age.
events.detail:
Using a known king of another land to fix a date is called a **synchronism**. Sri Lanka's chronicles date **Gajabahu I**, so Senguttuvan must be of the 2nd century CE.

Senguttuvan is said to have brought a stone from the Himalayas for the Kannagi image. His brother, by tradition, was **Ilango Adigal**, the author of the Silappadikaram.
events.source: NCERT Class 6 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 175 CE: Gajabahu I of Sri Lanka ruled about 171–193 CE.
events.before: The Cheras ruled the Kerala coast from **Vanji**, with the port of **Muziris** busy with Roman trade (about 60 CE).
events.after: By about 300 CE the Sangam kingdoms faded and the **Kalabhras** took over the Tamil land.
events.today: Kannagi (Pattini) is still worshipped in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka; the Attukal festival in Thiruvananthapuram is linked with her.

events.title: Mahendravarman I starts rock-cut temples in the Pallava land
events.summary: The Pallava king Mahendravarman I (about 600–630 CE) cuts the first rock-cut cave temples of the Tamil land, writes the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana, and turns from Jainism to Shaivism under the saint Appar.
events.detail:
His titles include **Vichitrachitta** ("curious-minded") and **Chaityakari** (temple-builder). His cave temple at **Mandagapattu** says it was made "without bricks, timber, metal or mortar" — something new.

He fought **Pulakeshin II** of Badami, who took Vengi and pressed on Kanchi. This began a long **Pallava–Chalukya war**.
events.source: NCERT Class 6, 7 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 610 CE: four years after Harsha takes the throne (606) and four years before Pulakeshin II's brother is placed at Vengi (624).
events.before: **Simhavishnu** (about 575 CE) had revived the Pallavas at Kanchi and taken the land up to the Kaveri.
events.after: His son **Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla)** avenged him by sacking the Chalukya capital **Vatapi** (642 CE) and built the rathas at **Mamallapuram**.
events.today: Cave temples of his time are at Mandagapattu, Mahendravadi and Dalavanur (Tamil Nadu). In Andhra, the **Undavalli** caves are older (Vishnukundin).
events.mnemonic: Pallava art in four steps by king "Mahendra → Mamalla → Rajasimha → Aparajita": caves → rathas → structural temples → late temples.
